claims.text: If an agent loses its workspace, does its memory come back, and do its written permissions still hold?
claims.quote: if an agent loses its workspace, does its memory come back, and do its written permissions still hold?

claims.text: Mondweep Chakravorty's video, published on YouTube on 17 October 2026, is 104.7 seconds long and replays a real terminal run in twelve steps.
claims.quote: It is 104.7 seconds long.

claims.text: Mondweep Chakravorty is a member of the Ruflo-Federation and co-founder of the Agentics Foundation's London chapter.
claims.quote: a member of the Ruflo-Federation and co-founder of the Agentics Foundation's London chapter

claims.text: The code is public under the MIT licence: a local MCP server of four tools, a strict compiler from an Agent Behaviour Policy to Ruflo rules, 16 tests and the evidence from each run.
claims.quote: a local MCP server of four tools, a strict compiler that turns an Agent Behaviour Policy into Ruflo rules, 16 tests, and the evidence from each run

claims.text: The analysis was made frame by frame in a separate session with Claude and checked against the code; every number comes from the video's timeline, a frame or the repository.
claims.quote: Every number below comes from the video's timeline, a frame or the repository.

claims.text: Step 1 pins the runtime: ruflo v3.56.10, the SGit source commit and the adapter version 0.2, which is what makes the run reproducible.
claims.quote: Pinning the versions is what makes a run like this reproducible.

claims.text: Step 2 defines four ABP rows scoped to the project: write, read and read history yes, delete memory approval; unsupported or ambiguous policies fail closed.
claims.quote: No raw rule overrides. Unsupported or ambiguous policies fail closed.

claims.text: The rows are compiled into Ruflo rules when the server starts, and every tool call is checked by a pinned copy of Ruflo's own policy evaluator in enforce mode.
claims.quote: every tool call is checked by a pinned copy of Ruflo's own policy evaluator, in enforce mode

claims.text: Step 3 stores two synthetic facts about Kestrel through Ruflo's own command line, with embeddings switched off.
claims.quote: Ruflo's own command line stores two synthetic facts, with embeddings switched off

claims.text: Step 4 asks the adapter to checkpoint a namespace called forbidden; it is refused with a PermissionError and nothing is written.
claims.quote: the run asks the adapter to checkpoint a namespace called forbidden

claims.text: Step 5 saves the checkpoint as a consistent SQLite backup with three SHA-256 fingerprints, of the database, the ABP and the compiled policy; only encrypted SGit bare objects enter the store.
claims.quote: Only encrypted SGit bare objects enter the checkpoint store. Private keys remain in a separate private directory.

claims.text: Binding the data to the rules in force, by fingerprinting the ABP and compiled policy alongside the database, is the detail the author likes most.
claims.quote: Binding the data to the rules in force is the detail I like most.

claims.text: Step 6 tries to close the run, which would delete memory; that row says approval and none is supplied, so it stops with a PermissionError and the checkpoint is retained.
claims.quote: That row says approval, and none is supplied, so it stops with a PermissionError

claims.text: Step 7 deletes the disposable test project; the loss is real, not simulated.
claims.quote: The loss is real, not simulated.

claims.text: Step 8 restores the checkpoint in a brand-new MCP server process into a workspace called fresh-runner; the database's SHA-256 is the same as in step 5.
claims.quote: a brand-new MCP server process restores the checkpoint into a workspace called fresh-runner

claims.text: Step 9 has Ruflo itself, not the adapter, read the restored memory, and both facts come back word for word, which makes the proof stronger than a demo that checks its own output.
claims.quote: PASS: both values match the CLI-written facts exactly.

claims.text: Step 10 looks up a key that was never stored and it stays missing: the restore did not invent anything, and the check can fail.
claims.quote: The restore did not invent anything, and the check can fail.

claims.text: Step 11 alters one encrypted checkpoint object; the restore fails with a ValueError because the adapter compares the ciphertext digest with the one recorded and refuses before decrypting.
claims.quote: the adapter compares the digest of the stored ciphertext with the one it recorded when it saved the checkpoint, and refuses before anything is decrypted

claims.text: Step 12's summary: exact recall PASS 2 of 2, ABP denial PASS, deletion needing approval BLOCKED with checkpoint retained, fresh-process restore PASS, tampered restore BLOCKED, semantic recall NOT VALIDATED.
claims.quote: exact recall PASS 2/2; ABP denial PASS; deletion that needs approval BLOCKED, checkpoint retained; fresh-process restore PASS; tampered restore BLOCKED

claims.text: The repository's acceptance runner has since validated keyword recall against Ruflo's real memory store; recall by meaning is partial because no vectors were stored even with embeddings on.
claims.quote: Recall by meaning is reported as partial, because no vectors were stored even with embeddings on

claims.text: What makes it more than a demo is the loop: store, save, delete for real, restore in a new process, read back with the original tool, test the refusals, include a negative control, and state the scope on screen.
claims.quote: Most "memory that persists" demos skip the deletion or reuse the same process.

claims.text: This is the first time someone outside our own sessions has run an encrypted vault as an agent's memory and a behaviour policy beside the prompt together inside someone else's agent stack, on camera.
claims.quote: This is the first time someone outside our own sessions has taken the two ideas we keep arguing for

claims.text: Two questions this piece does not answer: when is the vault actually used, and is every path to the memory guarded, since Ruflo's own command line reaches the memory file without the policy.
claims.quote: The run raises two questions this piece does not answer.

claims.text: The account is from the screen and the code: the audio was not transcribed, and the code was read, not run, by this site.
claims.quote: The audio was not transcribed; the code was read, not run, by this site.

claims.text: It is a proof of concept, not a product; reliability and real-world value are still to validate.
claims.quote: A proof of concept, not a product.

claims.text: Recall by meaning was not tested; exact recall was.
claims.quote: Recall by meaning was not tested. Exact recall was.

claims.text: The facts are synthetic; Kestrel is a test name, not a real fleet.
claims.quote: Kestrel is a test name, not a real fleet.

claims.text: The analysis is an AI's, made by Claude for the author and checked against the frames by the site's agent.
claims.quote: It was made by Claude for me and checked against the frames by this site's agent.

claims.text: The frames are Mondweep's and published with his agreement; the code was read at its commit of 16 October 2026; Ruflo is rUv's open-source agent orchestration under MIT.
claims.quote: published here with his agreement; the frames are his and are not covered by this site's licence
